newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Rats, warders outnumber Albania's prisoners.
newsitem.headline: Rats, warders outnumber Albania's prisoners.

text.p: Convicted killer Altin Koci curses his luck in a filthy cell in Tirana's main jail, where rats scamper and guards still far outnumber prisoners after an insurrection across Albania last month.
Strongly-built, Koci is one of just 16 people in jail since the Balkan state slid to the brink of anarchy last month. Albania's seven prisons were smashed and all 1,309 convicts escaped.

In a minor victory for struggling police, Koci was caught and locked up again in recent days in the prison, built after Benito Mussolini's fascists invaded Albania in 1939 by Italian architects who had a good grasp of medieval horror.

"My family brings me food, I don't like what they serve here," said Koci, 22, standing on the concrete floor of a tiny cell by a bag of sausages and cheese and facing the rest of a life sentence imposed two years ago.
A thin, grimy mattress and a blanket lie on the chill floor -- there is no chair or table. Koci's only decorations are big swastikas he has etched on the heavy wooden door.

Tiny barred windows in his cell, whose floor measures about two metres by four (six ft by 13), are too high to peer out of. Guards in blue uniforms far outnumber the 10 prisoners in the jail, littered with debris after rioting.
Yet the jail -- where stinking toilets are blocked, rats scurry in the corridors and one floor was wrecked by fire -- is one of two officially working prisons in Albania.
"The situation is still very grave," said Bedri Coku, director of Albania's prison system. "There is very low security in the prisons and law and order are not functioning properly."
Plastic bottles of yellow liquid lie in the abandoned cells -- prisoners get one bottle for water, the other for urine.
Coku said about 600 of the 1,309 people who escaped jail last month would be freed under an amnesty law passed by Albania's parliament on Wednesday night.

The law excludes serious crimes like murder, robbery, rape, "genocide" by former communists, state corruption or pimping. Criminals turning up voluntarily to jail by April 12 will get a third off the rest of their sentences.

Koci will not benefit from the amnesty -- guards said he was sentenced to death for robbing and shooting dead a money-changer in front of his wife. President Sali Berisha commuted the sentence to life.
Over the corridor from Koci, grey-haired Ahmet Zhullima, 75, lies on his mattress in his featureless white cell.

"Police came round to my house after we broke out of the jail and they asked me to come back. I agreed," he said. Serving a 10-year sentence for accidentally killing his son, he said he hoped to benefit from amnesty because of his age.
So far, 11 prisoners had returned of their own free will around the country, he said. Five have been arrested for new crimes -- a tiny dent in lawlesness and banditry.
"We probably have prison space in Tirana's two working jails for 400 people," Coku said.

Of Albania's other five jails, two are in areas run by rebels since last month's mayhem, triggered by anger at the failure of fradulent savings schemes this year. The other three are too badly damaged by attacks.
Coku hopes more prisoners will turn up as the April 12 deadline for applying for amnesty approaches. "Maybe they're waiting...I suppose they prefer to stay at home," he said.
